title: Who decides?
hookLine: a pope, councils of bishops, synods, or congregations: churches order authority differently

cards: The argument has traveled all the way from Antioch to Jerusalem. The church is young; the question is big: must believers who aren't Jewish take on the whole law of Moses, circumcision included, to follow Jesus?
Good people stand on both sides. So, in the fifteenth chapter of Acts, the apostles and elders come together. There's much disputing.
Peter tells what he's seen. Paul and Barnabas tell their stories. Then James gives his judgment.
And the letter they send out carries a sentence worth hearing slowly. Behind it sits today's question: who decides?

teach.h: IT SEEMED GOOD TO THE SPIRIT AND TO US.
teach.b: The letter says: "For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us." Both: the Spirit, and a room of people who argued. Churches across the traditions hold that hope: that their decisions can be human and holy at once.
But they've built that room very differently.

Catholics look to the pope, the bishop of Rome, as Peter's successor, with the bishops in communion with him; they read Jesus's words, "thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church," as founding that office.

teach.h: POPE AND BISHOPS; COUNCILS AND SYNODS.
teach.b: The Orthodox are governed by bishops in councils and synods, with patriarchs who lead without a single head over all, and see the council in Acts as their pattern.
Presbyterian and Reformed churches are led by elders, ruling together in local sessions and wider assemblies; they point to the elders in that chapter.
Baptists and other congregational churches gather the members to decide, trusting the Spirit to speak through the whole body, and notice that the apostles and elders acted with "the whole church."
Each can read Acts fifteen and see its own room. Under it all sits something Jesus said when two disciples asked for the best seats and the others were angry. Rulers lord it over people.

teach.h: THE GREAT ONE IS THE SERVANT.
teach.b: "But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister." A minister, in that old English, is a servant.
Paul adds: "Let all things be done decently and in order." In Christian teaching, order is meant to serve love: so the hungry get fed, the gospel gets told, and nobody gets trampled.

how: Catholics are led by the pope and bishops, Orthodox churches by bishops in synods, Presbyterian and Reformed churches by elders in sessions and assemblies, and Baptist and other congregational churches by the gathered members; churches often pray for their leaders by name in worship.

o: a vote on which hymns a church will sing
the question of how a church makes its decisions
a rule that a pastor's word is always final

games.q: who decides where — tap the pairs.

s: the council in Acts 15 decided without any argument
Acts says there was much disputing before Peter, Paul, Barnabas and James spoke.
the letter from Jerusalem names both the Holy Ghost and the people
"it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us."
Jesus told his disciples the greatest should rule over the rest
"whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister": a servant.

games.q: you're at the meeting in Jerusalem. the dispute is sharp and good people disagree. how does it get settled?
o: the loudest side wins the vote.
they listen to testimony, James gives judgment, and a letter goes out from all.
games.why: Peter, Paul and Barnabas tell what they've seen, James gives judgment, and the letter says "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us."

practice: Bring to mind whoever carries the decisions where you belong, a pastor or priest, a bishop, elders, a council, or, outside a church, a manager, a teacher, a parent. Picture them in a hard meeting where good people disagree.
If you pray, ask that their decisions seem good to the Holy Spirit and to them, and that they lead by serving; if you don't, just hold them kindly in that hard room.

wordCard.voice: Who decides? Popes and bishops, councils and synods, elders, whole congregations: different shapes of one hope, that the Spirit and the people agree.

orig.note: Greek: overseer — the New Testament word that English renders as bishop.

carryVoice: Your line: order for love. The great one among you is the servant. Until tomorrow.
